title: Detecting Molecular Residual Disease (MRD) Changes What You Can See and When You Can Act
summary: How Labcorp Plasma Detect® Genome MRD for Colon Cancer (Stage III) brings ctDNA surveillance to post-treatment workflows
body_markdown:
## The problem standard surveillance doesn’t solve


One of the most critical challenges in the evolution of oncology remains the early identification of cancer recurrence. For patients with stage III colon cancer, this is particularly urgent. A[systematic review](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/cam4.6884) of randomized controlled trials indicates that recurrence rates can be as high as 30% for patients with stage III colorectal cancer after curative surgery and adjuvant chemotherapy.1-3


## MRD testing is becoming the new benchmark in recurrence risk assessment


MRD refers to the subclinical presence of microscopic cancer that persists after surgery or definitive treatment. It is undetectable by physical exam or standard imaging techniques, yet its detection suggests a high risk of disease recurrence.4-5 For oncologists managing post-treatment surveillance, circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) based MRD detection offers a real-time, molecular view of whether disease is truly absent or simply below the detection threshold of conventional surveillance tools.


The clinical signal from ctDNA is compelling. Studies have demonstrated that ctDNA-positive result following curative-intent surgery is a powerful, independent predictor of recurrence risk in colorectal cancer. Ongoing clinical trials are evaluating precisely how MRD status should guide decisions regarding adjuvant therapy escalation and de-escalation, with early data suggesting that MRD-guided approaches may reduce overtreatment in low-risk patients while accelerating intervention in those at highest risk.6-7


Regulatory and scientific momentum is building as well. The Blood Profiling Atlas in Cancer (BloodPAC) Consortium and key regulatory bodies have issued consensus guidance emphasizing the need for standardized MRD testing methods and consistent clinical terminology. This signals growing momentum toward standardized MRD testing and broader clinical integration.


For oncologists treating solid tumors, the question is no longer whether MRD testing is clinically meaningful. The question is which platform delivers the sensitivity, speed, and workflow integration to make it actionable.
